Overview

Sample data. This trial is generated by tools/synthetic_trial.py (seed 7) from known true effects. It is not a real experiment. Because the truth is known, every estimate on this page can be compared with it; where a result is a property of the simulator rather than of salmon, the page says so.

2 diets were compared in 8 tanks in 4 RAS systems, 2 per temperature level. The tank is the experimental unit, so every test below uses one number per tank.

Primary outcome: growth_sgr

Does the diet change the growth rate of a tank over the trial? D2 − D1 = 0.118 % per day (95 % interval -0.005 to 0.241), p = 0.054 with 2 error degrees of freedom: not shown at the 5 % level.

The generator's true effect is 0.125 % per day; the estimate lies 0.24 standard errors from it and the interval contains it. What the trial lacks is precision: with 2 systems per temperature level the standard error rests on 2 degrees of freedom, and an estimate must exceed 4.30 standard errors (not about 2) to count as significant. See Statistics for each test and Power and design for what more systems would change.

Statistics

Every analysis below was fixed in the plan before the trial started (table planned_outcomes) and is computed by tools/analysis.py, which reads the plan and runs exactly the registered models. Each analysis has automated tests; see Evidence.

How to read the tests

1. The experimental unit is the tank, never the fish

Diets were allocated to tanks. Fish of one tank share water, feed and each other, so they are not independent observations of a diet. Every test therefore uses one number per tank (8 tanks). Weighing more fish makes a tank's number more precise; it does not add replicates. What happens when this is ignored is shown under The analysis not to run.

2. Two layers of allocation, two error terms (split plot)

Temperature was set per system, diet per tank inside a system. The analysis keeps the two layers apart:

  • Temperature is compared with the variation between systems kept at the same level. There are 4 systems and 2 levels, so this yardstick has 4 − 2 = 2 degrees of freedom.
  • Diet and diet × temperature use the difference between the two diets inside each system. The system itself cancels out of that difference. The yardstick is how much the difference varies between systems of the same level: again 2 degrees of freedom.

Testing temperature against tanks would treat the tanks of one system as independent, the same mistake as treating fish as replicates, one level up. Rule R35 of the data model checks every planned model for this, and the plan of this trial names system as an error stratum.

3. What each test computes: t, F, p and the 95 % interval

Each test compares an estimated difference with its standard error (SE), the amount by which the estimate would vary between repetitions of the trial: t = estimate / SE. For a factor with two levels the F ratio of the ANOVA table is t².

  • Null hypothesis: the true difference is 0 (the ratio is 1).
  • p value: the probability, if the null hypothesis were true and the assumptions hold, of a t at least as far from 0 as the one observed. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
  • Decision rule fixed in the plan: two-sided, alpha = 0.05. A p below alpha is called significant.
  • 95 % interval: estimate ± tcrit × SE, the true differences that are compatible with the data. An interval that contains 0 (or ratio 1) goes with a p above alpha.
4. Why 2 degrees of freedom dominate every result here

The SE is itself estimated, here from only 2 independent pieces of information. The t distribution compensates by asking for more: an estimate must exceed 4.30 × SE to be significant, instead of 1.96 × SE with a well-estimated SE. An interval built on these degrees of freedom is therefore 2.2 times as wide as it would be with the same SE known exactly. The multiplier falls to 2.78 with 3 systems per level and 2.45 with 4 systems per level.

This is a property of the design, fixed before any fish was weighed. No analysis method recovers the missing information.

5. Scales: difference, ratio, odds ratio
  • raw: the contrast is a difference in the unit of the metric.
  • log: the natural log of the tank value is analysed; a difference of logs is a ratio, so exp(estimate) is reported: 1.18 means 18 % more, 0.95 means 5 % less. Totals such as feed and gain vary in proportion to their size, which the log scale makes additive.
  • logit (survival): ln((alive + 0.5) / (dead + 0.5)) per tank from the d0 count; the 0.5 keeps a tank without deaths finite. exp(estimate) is an odds ratio of surviving.
6. Feed conversion without analysing a ratio

The data model's rule for FCR is: fit feed and gain, do not analyse the ratio. Feed eaten (intake_log) and gain (gain_log) are analysed separately. On the log scale feed per gain is their difference, so its diet contrast is exactly the intake contrast minus the gain contrast: 0.1157 − 0.1677 = -0.0520, and feed_per_gain_log reports -0.0520. Taken per tank, the difference keeps the link between a tank's feed and its own gain, which two separate tests cannot use. The raw FCR ratio is never put into a test.

7. Randomisation test: the same question without assuming a distribution

The diets were allocated at random to the two tanks of each system. If diet changed nothing in any tank, swapping the two labels inside a system would have been just as likely. With 4 systems there are 16 equally likely allocations; the p value is the share of them whose diet effect is at least as large as the one observed. Nothing is assumed about the distribution of the data. The price: p cannot go below 0.125 here, so this test can never reach significance in this design, whatever the data. See Randomisation test.

8. Several outcomes: Holm adjustment

Testing 4 secondary outcomes at 5 % each would give a false positive somewhere more often than 5 % of the time. The plan names the Holm method for this family: the smallest p is multiplied by 4, the next by 3, and so on, never letting an adjusted value fall below the one before it. Calling only adjusted p values below alpha significant keeps the chance of any false positive in the family at 5 % at most. The primary outcome stands alone and is not adjusted.

9. Sensitivity analysis: the pending exclusion

An exclusion that nobody has decided yet stays in the primary analysis (intention to treat). A sensitivity analysis repeats the contrasts without that tank. Its system then has no within-system diet difference and drops out, which leaves fewer degrees of freedom. The result is reported for every outcome so that the reader can see whether the conclusion depends on that tank.

10. Assumptions, and which of them could be checked
  • Independent units: holds by design when allocation was random; the randomisation runs are recorded in the database (see Design and plan).
  • Normal errors with equal variance: cannot be assessed with 2 error degrees of freedom. No residual plot or normality test has any power here, so none is shown. Two things stand in for it: the randomisation test (no distribution assumed), and the simulation evidence. In 120 synthetic trials whose tank noise is uniform, not normal, the 95 % interval covered the true effect 112 times (93 %), and in 120 trials with no diet effect the test rejected 5 times.
  • No interference between the tanks of a system: tanks on one loop share water, so one diet could reach the neighbouring tank through water quality. The design assumes it does not; these data cannot show whether it did.
11. 'Not significant' is not 'no effect'

The design was planned to find a diet difference of 0.1 with 80 % power, given an SD between tanks of 0.025. Smaller true differences will usually not reach significance, and for the diet × temperature interaction the smallest difference found with that power is 0.20. A non-significant result therefore says the trial could not tell; the interval says what remains possible.

  • Plan check: the plan declares 80 % power for a difference of 0.1; recomputed from its SD and this design: 80.0 % (consistent).

  • Variation: SD between tanks of a system 0.00193 (95 % interval 0.00101 to 0.0121, from 2 df); between-system SD 0.00174.

Sample-data note. The generator gives every tank of a diet the same feed efficiency on feeding days (0.80 for D1 and 0.76 for D2) with no variation between tanks, so the SE here is far smaller than a real trial would give. The size of the effect is meaningful; the tiny p value is a property of the simulator.

Reading

  • Diet (D2 - D1, mean over temperature): odds ratio 0.917, 95 % interval 0.311 to 2.703; t = -0.34 on 2 df, p = 0.763, Holm-adjusted p = 0.763: not shown at the 5 % level.
  • Does the diet effect depend on temperature? Diet effect at one level divided by that at the other: odds ratio 0.439 (0.051 to 3.813), p = 0.243: no dependence is shown, and none is ruled out. This is the least precise contrast of the design (its SE is twice that of the diet effect).
  • Temperature (16C - 12C, mean over diets), tested against systems: odds ratio 1.478 (0.411 to 5.318), p = 0.320.
  • Randomisation test of the diet effect: p = 1.000, from 16 allocations; the smallest value this design allows is 0.125.
  • Without the pending exclusion (U2D2): diet odds ratio 0.888 (0.004 to 214.184) on 3 systems and 1 df, p = 0.830.
  • Variation: SD between tanks of a system 0.355 (95 % interval 0.185 to 2.23, from 2 df); between-system SD 0.159.

Sample-data note. The generator gives every tank the same chance of a death per day (0.04), whatever the diet or temperature. There is no true effect, so any difference here is chance.

Reading

  • Diet: estimate 2.0000; the error variance is numerically zero (rounding only), so no test is made.
  • Randomisation test of the diet effect: p = 0.125, from 16 allocations; the smallest value this design allows is 0.125.

Sample-data note. The generator fixes digestibility per diet without measurement noise, so tanks of a diet differ only by rounding. An F ratio on rounding noise would be meaningless and is withheld.

The analysis not to run: fish as replicates

The same final weights analysed twice (ln individual weight (g) at the end occasion). With every fish as an independent observation (160 fish): t = 10.6 on 156 degrees of freedom, p < 0.0001. With the tank mean as the observation (8 tanks): t = 3.75 on 2 degrees of freedom, p = 0.064. The first analysis claims 78 times the degrees of freedom the design has, and its SE is 2.8 times too small.

That this is wrong and not merely cautious is shown by trials generated with no diet effect at all: treating fish as replicates declared a significant diet effect in 57 of 120 trials (48 %); the tank analysis in 5 of 120. A test at the 5 % level should do so in about 5 %.

Randomisation test

Observed diet effect 0.118; 2 of the 16 allocations are at least as extreme, p = 0.125. The smallest p this test can give depends only on the number of systems: 4 systems → 0.1250, 6 systems → 0.0312, 8 systems → 0.0078, 12 systems → 0.0005. For temperature the systems themselves are permuted: 6 allocations, smallest possible p 0.333, so the temperature result of this trial rests entirely on the normal-theory test.

The SD between tanks actually observed for this outcome is 0.040, with a 95 % interval from 0.021 to 0.254: with 2 degrees of freedom a single trial says little about its own variability, which is why the plan's SD should come from historical trials (tools/calibrate_params.py).

Check of the power formula against simulation: at the generator's true effect the formula gives 91.7 %; 106 of 120 simulated trials (88.3 %) were significant. The standard error of such a share over 120 trials is 2.5 percentage points, and the generator's noise is uniform where the formula assumes normal.

A note on mixed-model software

The same tank values fitted as a mixed model with a random system effect (REML, statsmodels 0.15.0) give the same estimates, standard errors and variance components wherever the system variance is positive (see Evidence). What differs is the default test: a Wald z test treats the SE as known exactly and ignores that it rests on 2 degrees of freedom.

OutcomeStratum t test (plan)Wald z (default)lmerTest SatterthwaitelmerTest Kenward-RogerREML system variance
growth_sgr0.054 (df 2)< 0.00010.0055 (df 4)0.032 (df 2)1.02e-13 (at 0)
intake_log0.080 (df 2)0.00090.080 (df 2)0.080 (df 2)0.00419
gain_log0.038 (df 2)< 0.00010.038 (df 2)0.038 (df 2)0.0044
feed_per_gain_log0.0007 (df 2)< 0.00010.0007 (df 2)0.0007 (df 2)3.01e-06
survival_logit0.763 (df 2)0.7300.763 (df 2)0.763 (df 2)0.0254

p value of the diet effect. With 8 tanks the choice of reference distribution decides the conclusion; the stratum test is the one registered in the plan.

lme4 1.1.35.1 with lmerTest 3.1.3, the small-sample tests most mixed-model analyses report, give the stratum test's df and p wherever the system variance is positive. Where REML puts it at 0 (growth_sgr) the fit is singular: the system and tank error terms are pooled, Satterthwaite then counts the degrees of freedom of both, and Kenward-Roger keeps the df but uses the pooled variance. For the diet effect both p values are then smaller than that of the planned test, which keeps the design's own error term even when the system variance is estimated below 0; the planned test is the one shown under Evidence to reject at its nominal 5 % rate when there is no effect.

Tests of the statistical analyses

66 checks, 0 failed; 15 of 15 analyses are exercised. Each analysis is tested against something it did not compute itself:

  • Known truth. The synthetic trial is generated from known effects. Over repeated trials the estimates must be unbiased and the 95 % intervals must cover the truth about 95 % of the time; per trial, an estimate from the measured data must equal the same estimate from the generator's true tank values.
  • Independent implementation. The ANOVA against R (aov with an error stratum), estimates and variance components against a REML mixed model, contrasts with their degrees of freedom and p values against lme4/lmerTest (Satterthwaite and Kenward-Roger), F tests against least squares, the randomisation tests against brute-force relabelling, the power function against Monte-Carlo draws.
  • No effect. With nothing to find, a test at the 5 % level must reject about 5 % of the time.
  • Known wrong method. Fish as replicates must be shown to fail that requirement.

Mean estimate over 120 trials: 0.1248 (true 0.125). The 95 % interval covers the truth in 112 trials (93 %). The test is significant in 106 of them (88 %); with no diet effect in the generator it is significant in 5 of 120.

Limits

  • The data are simulated. The generator is simpler than a fish tank: tanks of a cell differ by a uniform ±3 % in growth rate, there is no variation between systems beyond that of their tanks, none between tanks in feed efficiency or digestibility, and the same mortality everywhere. Results marked with a sample-data note reflect this.
  • Few replicates. 2 systems per level leave 2 degrees of freedom for every test. The trial can show large effects only; see Power and design.
  • Scope of the analysis module. One whole-plot factor (or none), one tank per diet in each system (replicate tanks are averaged), each diet against the reference diet. Not implemented: growth curves over more than two weighings as repeated measures, time-to-event models of mortality, dose-response on analysed dose, ordinal models for welfare scores, pooling of several trials. The schema stores what these need; the code for them is not written.
  • Assumptions that cannot be checked here. Normality and equal variance of tank-level errors (see Statistics, point 10).
  • Adjusted analyses. No covariate adjustment is made; the plan lists start weight as a precision covariate, and with 8 tanks a covariate would use up one of the 2 error degrees of freedom.
  • This page. Static HTML with embedded charts; it does not update itself. Rebuild it with python tools/build_dashboard.py after any change to the data.
